title: Looking back: the Tenth Guru's pen

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the Gurus' teachings: Nanak talking with the yogis, the Gurus' different voices, the Ninth Guru's calm. Your line was many voices. Which voice stayed with you? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

Before sunrise, in a Sikh home, someone is reading quickly. The lines are short, and they land like footsteps: no mark, no sign, no caste, no lineage. That's the Jaap Sahib, and it comes from the pen of Guru Gobind Singh. That evening the same family stands for the Ardas, and its opening lines are his as well. And at an amrit ceremony, his words are read over the water while it is stirred. This year we spent a whole block with the Tenth Guru's writings: praise, a life story, a letter of rebuke, a love song. Today we look back at them from a different side. Not as a shelf of books, but as a voice still heard in a Sikh's day.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE: SHORT LINES, LIKE FOOTSTEPS.` → `EVENING: THE ARDAS.` → `THE AMRIT.`

segments.voice: Start at dawn. The Sikh code lists the morning prayers: Guru Nanak's Japji, and then two from the Tenth Guru, the Jaap Sahib and the Tav Prasad Swayye. So a morning can move from the First Guru's voice to the Tenth's without a pause. And his part is praise, name after name for the Timeless One, as if no single name could ever be enough. Then evening. The Rehras, the evening prayer in the code, carries his Chaupai. In paraphrase it begins: protect me with Your own hand, and let the wish of my heart be fulfilled. The warrior who wrote it asks to be held. Then the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say standing together. It opens with the first stanza of his Chandi di Var: first remember Bhagauti, the divine power, then Guru Nanak, and the Gurus after him. Bhagauti can be read as God's power, and some readers also hear the sword in that word. Either way, the shared prayer opens with strength and remembrance side by side. Then the amrit. The code names five prayers to be read as the water is stirred with a double-edged khanda, and three of the five are his: Jaap, the swayyas, the Chaupai. Pen and steel, in one bowl. The life story, the rebuke in the Zafarnama, the song from the wilderness: those are read and sung too, in katha and kirtan. But looking back, this is what stands out. His writings aren't only admired from a distance. They're said aloud, in the morning, at night, standing in prayer, and over the water of the Khalsa.
screen: `DAWN: JAAP AND THE SWAYYAS.` · `EVENING: THE CHAUPAI.` · `THE ARDAS OPENS WITH HIS STANZA.` · `THREE OF FIVE AT THE AMRIT.` · then, large: `PEN AND STEEL, IN ONE BOWL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line of his. Settle, and breathe. Here is the opening of the Jaap Sahib, in paraphrase: the One who has no mark and no sign, no caste and no lineage. Say it slowly, once, aloud or silently. Then let it sit. Notice which word stays with you: mark, sign, caste, lineage. All the labels people pin on one another, and the line pins none of them on God. If you pray, you can let the line be your praise. If not, just let it rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today, at the Tenth Guru's pen: his lines open the morning, fill the evening, begin the Ardas and stir the amrit. Today's word.
Your line: pen and sword. Today, watch for one moment that needs both: a gentle word and a firm one, held in the same hand. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the daily prayers read the Tenth Guru's Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Swayye in the morning and his Chaupai within the evening Rehras; the Ardas opens with his stanza from Chandi di Var.

Editor pass: changed 'Sikhs read Bhagauti as God's power' (a claim about all Sikhs) to 'Bhagauti can be read as God's power'; the rest checked against the cited Rehat Maryada and Dasam Granth passages and left as written.

Please confirm the Rehat Maryada's Nitnem list (morning: Japji, Jaap, Tav Prasad Swayye; evening: Rehras, which includes the Chaupai) and the five banis of the amrit ceremony (Japji, Jaap, Tav Prasad Swayye, Chaupai, Anand Sahib), of which three are from the Dasam Granth.
Bhagauti in the Ardas's opening: glossed as God's power, with 'some readers also hear the sword'. Please confirm the framing is fair.
Paraphrase of the Chaupai's opening (hamri karo hath dai rachha, puran hoe chit ki ichha) should be checked.
Gurmukhi ਜਾਪੁ (with aunkar) and pronunciation should be checked.
Authorship of parts of the Dasam Granth is discussed among Sikhs (days 1222, 1248); the compositions named here are the ones the Rehat Maryada itself uses.
